questions.explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma of the bronchus is strongly linked to tobacco smoking, whereas Burkitt/NPC (EBV), penile SCC (HPV), and HCC (HBV/HCV) have viral etiologies.

questions.stem: A 14-Years old elementary school teacher presents with fever, sore throat, and diffuse lacy rash she subsequently develop arthralgia of small joints of the hand what is the etiology:
questions.explanation: Parvovirus B19 (Fifth disease / erythema infectiosum) causes a lacy reticular rash and symmetrical small-joint polyarthralgia/arthritis in adults (especially teachers/women).

questions.stem: A 10 years old child comes to the clinic complaining of fever of 2 days duration, sore throat and fatigue. He reports that there is painful swelling in his neck. His CBC shows lymphocytosis with many atypical cells. What is the appropriate treatment of this patient?
questions.explanation: Pharyngitis, cervical lymphadenopathy, fatigue, and atypical lymphocytosis (Downey cells) indicate EBV infectious mononucleosis, which requires symptomatic supportive care.

questions.stem: Contamination with contact lenses could lead to eye infection with:
questions.explanation: Acanthamoeba castellanii is a free-living amoeba found in tap water/soil that causes severe, painful vision-threatening keratitis in contact lens wearers.

questions.stem: River blindness is a clinical manifestation of infection with:
questions.explanation: Onchocerca volvulus (transmitted by Simulium blackflies breeding near fast-flowing rivers) causes onchocerciasis ('river blindness').

questions.stem: River blindness is caused by:
questions.explanation: Ocular pathology and blindness in onchocerciasis result from host inflammatory reactions to dying microfilariae of Onchocerca volvulus migrating through the cornea and anterior chamber.

questions.stem: Ocular cysticercosis is caused by:
options: Ingestion of undercooked pork containing cysticercous cellulose.
Ingestion of food or water containing egg of Taenia solium.
External autoinfection in a patient has Taeniasis saginata.
Ingestion of undercooked beef containing cysticercous bovis.
Ingestion of undercooked beef containing cysticercous cellulose.
questions.explanation: Cysticercosis (neuro- and ocular) develops when humans ingest Taenia solium EGGS via fecal-oral contamination (whereas eating undercooked pork larvae causes intestinal taeniasis).

questions.stem: Subcutaneous nodules are a typical finding in:
questions.explanation: Adult Onchocerca volvulus worms become encapsulated in fibrous subcutaneous nodules called onchocercomas, typically over bony prominences.

questions.stem: One of the following is a cause of blindness in tropics
questions.explanation: Onchocerciasis is a leading infectious cause of preventable blindness in tropical sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America.

questions.stem: Which of the following parasites may cause keratitis:
questions.explanation: Acanthamoeba causes destructive amoebic keratitis with radial perineuritis and ring-shaped corneal infiltrates.

questions.stem: Toxocariasis of the eye is typically presented with which of the following eye signs:
questions.explanation: Ocular larva migrans (Toxocara canis) classically presents in children as unilateral posterior uveitis/chorioretinitis with a posterior pole granuloma and leukocoria.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the route of eye infection with toxoplasmosis:
questions.explanation: Ocular toxoplasmosis (chorioretinitis) most commonly results from congenital transplacental (mother-to-child) transmission, reactivating later in childhood or young adulthood.

questions.stem: River blindness is due to:
questions.explanation: River blindness is the common clinical name for Onchocerciasis caused by the filarial nematode Onchocerca volvulus.

questions.stem: Improper contact lens-care practices may lead to:
questions.explanation: Washing contact lenses with tap water or swimming while wearing lenses exposes the cornea to Acanthamoeba keratitis.

questions.stem: Retinochoroiditis is caused by eye infection with:
questions.explanation: Toxoplasma gondii is the most common infectious cause of posterior uveitis / focal necrotizing retinochoroiditis.

questions.stem: All the following intestinal nematodes inhabit the large intestine except:
questions.explanation: Ascaris lumbricoides (as well as hookworms and Strongyloides) inhabits the SMALL intestine, whereas Trichuris trichiura and Enterobius vermicularis inhabit the large intestine.

questions.stem: The following parasite enters human body via skin:
questions.explanation: Hookworm (Ancylostoma duodenale / Necator americanus) infective filariform (L3) larvae penetrate intact human skin (usually bare feet).

questions.stem: All of the following tapeworms are transmitted by ingestion of undercooked meat, EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Echinococcus granulosus is acquired by ingesting tapeworm eggs shed in dog feces, NOT by eating undercooked meat.

questions.stem: In treatment of taeniasis solium it is preferable to use:
questions.explanation: Niclosamide is non-absorbable and kills adult intestinal worms without damaging eggs or crossing into tissue cysts (avoiding neurocysticercosis inflammatory reactions if occult cysts exist).

questions.stem: Which of the following parasites inhabits large intestine:
questions.explanation: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) resides in the cecum and appendix of the large intestine; Ascaris, Strongyloides, and Ancylostoma inhabit the small intestine.

questions.stem: One of The following is not recognized cause of eosinophilia
questions.explanation: Visceral leishmaniasis (an intracellular protozoan) causes pancytopenia with eosinopenia, whereas invasive helminths (Toxocara, Schistosoma) and drug reactions cause marked eosinophilia.

questions.stem: A 20 year old man who presented with persistent diarrhea and abdominal bloating after returning from a gap year in Africa is diagnosed as having strongyloidiasis. How the Strongyloides stercoralis organism would initially entered his body?
questions.explanation: Strongyloides stercoralis infective filariform larvae in contaminated soil penetrate human skin directly.

questions.stem: Diagnosis of trichinosis by:
options: Detection of larvae in blood in first week.
Detection of larvae in stool in first week.
Detection of larvae in muscle biopsy in first week.
Detection of larvae in CSF in first week.
questions.explanation: Definitive parasitological diagnosis of Trichinella spiralis infection is made by identifying encysted larvae in striated skeletal muscle biopsy (supported by serology and eosinophilia).

questions.stem: Duodenal aspirate is helpful in diagnosis of:
questions.explanation: Because Strongyloides stercoralis eggs hatch into rhabditiform larvae within the duodenal mucosa, duodenal aspiration (or Entero-Test) has high sensitivity when stool exams are negative.

questions.stem: Cysticercosis is the larval stage of:
questions.explanation: Cysticercus cellulosae is the tissue-invading larval stage of the pork tapeworm Taenia solium.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain. He states that the symptoms are worse with eating, and that his abdominal pain has been increasing over the past three to four months. He reports a history of travel to endemic area with parasites five months ago. After that he developed a cough associated with mild shortness of breath which he attributed to a viral respiratory infection, as it resolved shortly thereafter. His physical examination is significant for moderate periumbilical tenderness. His laboratory results are significant for an eosinophil count of 20 percent. A CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed small bowel dilation proximal to a whirlpool-like mass in the mid-jejunum causing intestinal obstruction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Initial pulmonary larval migration (Löffler's pneumonitis), 20% eosinophilia, and a tangled bolus of large worms causing small-bowel obstruction are classic for Ascaris lumbricoides.

questions.stem: All of the following are clinical manifestations of Ascaris lumbricoides infection except:
options: fever, headache, photophobia, neck rigidity, and eosinophilia
non-productive cough and pleurisy with eosinophilia
right upper quadrant pain and fever
questions.explanation: Ascaris causes Löffler's pneumonitis, biliary/pancreatic duct obstruction (RUQ pain), and small-bowel obstruction, but does NOT typically cause acute bacterial-like meningitis.

questions.stem: All the following are true regarding leptospirosis except:
options: Lice act as reservoirs of infection
questions.explanation: Rodents (especially rats) are the primary reservoirs shedding Leptospira in urine; lice play no role in transmission.

questions.stem: Leptospirosis is commonly associated with exposure to:
questions.explanation: Leptospira interrogans is acquired through contact with freshwater, soil, or mud contaminated with infected animal (rodent/livestock) urine.

questions.stem: How is leptospirosis transmitted?
options: Exposure of mucous membranes or abraded skin to the contaminated water
By contact with the infected person
questions.explanation: Spirochetes enter the host via abraded skin or intact mucous membranes (conjunctiva, oral/nasal mucosa) exposed to urine-contaminated water.

questions.stem: How is Leptospirosis treated for humans?
questions.explanation: Mild leptospirosis is treated with oral Doxycycline or Amoxicillin; severe Weil's disease requires IV Penicillin G or Ceftriaxone.

questions.stem: Which of the following laboratory results is common in severe form of leptospirosis:
questions.explanation: Thrombocytopenia (often accompanied by elevated bilirubin, transaminases, and creatinine) is a hallmark laboratory abnormality in severe leptospirosis.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old farmer presents with headache, fever, myalgia, nausea, oliguria and subconjunctival hemorrhage. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Agricultural/water exposure, fever, calf myalgias, conjunctival suffusion/hemorrhage, and oliguric renal injury define severe Leptospirosis (Weil's disease).

questions.stem: The most consistent pathologic finding in leptospirosis is:
questions.explanation: Leptospires damage small blood vessel endothelium, causing systemic infectious capillary vasculitis responsible for conjunctival suffusion, renal failure, and hemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old sewage worker presents with 3 days history of low back pain, fever, myalgia, fatigue, jaundice, subconjunctival hemorrhage and renal impairment. He has no past medical history and has not been abroad in the last 6 months. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sewage workers are at high occupational risk for leptospirosis; jaundice + renal failure + subconjunctival hemorrhage is classic Weil's syndrome.

questions.stem: Which are not portals of entry for the organism in leptospirosis:
questions.explanation: Leptospira enters via abraded skin, mucous membranes, and conjunctiva; sexual contact is not a recognized transmission route.

questions.stem: Which are the two types of leptospirosis?
questions.explanation: Clinically, leptospirosis is divided into the mild, self-limiting Anicteric form (~90%) and the severe Icteric form (Weil's disease, ~10%).

questions.stem: Which form of leptospirosis is known as Weil's disease?
questions.explanation: Weil's disease refers specifically to the severe icteric form of leptospirosis characterized by jaundice, renal dysfunction, and hemorrhagic diathesis.

questions.stem: The following symptoms and signs are true regarding anicteric leptospirosis except?
questions.explanation: Leptospirosis causes non-purulent conjunctival suffusion (redness without pus), NOT exudative/purulent conjunctivitis.

questions.stem: Which pathogen is known for forming spores and causing difficult-to-eradicate hospital acquired diarrhea?
questions.explanation: Clostridioides difficile forms hardy, alcohol-resistant spores that persist on hospital surfaces and cause antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitis.

questions.stem: What laboratory methods are available to diagnose patients with suspected Clostridium difficile infection?
options: Stool toxin test (toxin A and B enzyme immunoassay)
questions.explanation: Multi-step diagnostic algorithms utilize GDH screening, Toxin A/B EIA, and NAAT (PCR) for toxin genes on unformed stool.

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms are most likely to cause bloody diarrhea and fever in an international traveler?
questions.explanation: Invasive bacterial enteropathogens such as Salmonella enterica, Shigella, and Campylobacter cause febrile inflammatory/bloody traveler's diarrhea.

questions.stem: Which agent is the usual choice for moderate to severe travelers' diarrhea?
questions.explanation: Fluoroquinolones (such as Norfloxacin or Ciprofloxacin) or Azithromycin are standard antimicrobial choices for moderate-to-severe traveler's diarrhea.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy and his parents present with a 4-day history of oily, foul smelling diarrhea after a camping trip. Which medication is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Foul-smelling, greasy/oily steatorrhea following camping/untreated stream water exposure indicates Giardiasis, treated with Metronidazole (or Tinidazole).

questions.stem: 44 old man coming from trip to Pakistan 15 days ago complaining of watery non bloody diarrhea with abdominal bloating with no fever what is the diagnosis:
questions.explanation: Subacute non-bloody, afebrile diarrhea with prominent bloating and flatulence 1–2 weeks after travel is typical of Giardia lamblia.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most unlikely to be found in Clostridium difficile infection:
questions.explanation: C. difficile typically causes watery, foul-smelling diarrhea with leukocytosis and fever; grossly bloody diarrhea is uncommon and suggests alternative etiologies.

questions.stem: The characters of stool in giardiasis are:
questions.explanation: Giardia trophozoites coat the duodenal brush border causing malabsorption of fats, resulting in greasy, foul-smelling stools containing fat and mucus.

questions.stem: Which is not a recognised complication of acute shigellosis?
questions.explanation: Shigellosis can be complicated by HUS (S. dysenteriae type 1 Shiga toxin), reactive arthritis (Reiter's), and toxic megacolon, whereas amoebiasis causes liver abscess.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old student presents with a fifteen-week history of diarrhoea. He has lost 2 kg in weight, and has no recent travel abroad. A smear of a duodenal biopsy reveals many trophozoites. What is the best treatment option?
questions.explanation: Pear-shaped binucleate trophozoites on duodenal smear confirm chronic Giardiasis, treated effectively with Metronidazole.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding Clostridium difficile-associated disease relapses is true?
options: A first recurrence does not imply greater risk of further recurrences.
Most recurrences are due to antibiotic resistance.
Recurrent C. difficile-associated disease has been associated with a higher risk of colon cancer.
Recurrent disease is associated with serious complications.
Testing for clearance of C. difficile is warranted after treating recurrences.
questions.explanation: Recurrent C. difficile infection carries significant risk of severe morbidity, dehydration, sepsis, and toxic megacolon (test-of-cure is not recommended).

questions.stem: Microbial flora of Gl tract does not contain
questions.explanation: Klebsiella ozaenae is an upper respiratory pathogen associated with atrophic rhinitis (ozena), not a normal commensal of the GI tract.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a part of standard precautions?
questions.explanation: Hand hygiene is the single most important component of Standard Precautions applied to all patients regardless of suspected infection status.

questions.stem: Alcohol-based hand rubs are ineffective against:
questions.explanation: Alcohol-based hand sanitizers do NOT kill bacterial spores (such as Clostridioides difficile); mechanical handwashing with soap and water is required.

questions.stem: Who is responsible for implementing Infection Prevention and Control?
questions.explanation: Every individual healthcare worker is directly responsible for implementing IPC practices at the point of patient care.

questions.stem: A frontline doctor is infected with hepatitis B while at work due to a needle stick injury. What is the legal position of the infection?
options: Ask him to follow standard precautions
questions.explanation: A bloodborne infection acquired via a percutaneous sharps injury during clinical duties is legally classified as an occupational and work-related injury.

questions.stem: What infection prevention and control measures should be used with patients with Clostridium difficile infection?
options: Donning of gloves and gowns by health care providers
Hand washing with soap and water
Isolation of asymptomatic carriers of C. difficile
questions.explanation: Because C. difficile spores resist alcohol, handwashing with soap and water (along with contact precautions—gloves & gowns) is essential.

questions.stem: The nurse must assign a room to a patient with scabies which of the following is the best option for this patient:
options: A semiprivate room with any patient
A room with another patient of scabies
questions.explanation: Scabies requires Contact Precautions in a private single-occupancy room until 24 hours after initiation of effective scabicide therapy.

questions.stem: The chain of infection has five main components. The habitat in which the agent normally lives, grows, and multiplies is known as the:
questions.explanation: The reservoir is the natural habitat (human, animal, or environmental) in which an infectious agent normally lives, grows, and multiplies.

questions.stem: Your patient is on airborne isolation and he will undergo ultrasound guided thoracocentesis. how will you advise the attendant nurse who will transport him:
options: N95 mask on the patient during transport out the room as well as the accompanying personnel
Surgical mask on the patient during transport out the room as well as the accompanying personnel
N95 mask on the patient, surgical mask for the accompanying personnel
Surgical mask on the patient, N95 Mask for the accompanying personnel
questions.explanation: During transport outside an airborne isolation room, the patient wears a surgical mask (to contain respiratory secretions) while accompanying staff wear N95 respirators.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a new nursing assistant about ways to prevent the spread of infection, included in the instruction would be that the cycle of the infectious process must be broken, which may be:
options: Hand washing before and between providing client care
Wearing infection control-approved protective equipment when providing patient care
Using medical and surgical aseptic techniques at all times
questions.explanation: Breaking the chain of infection requires multi-modal adherence: hand hygiene, environmental disinfection, proper PPE, and strict aseptic technique.

questions.stem: Standard precautions are important in:
options: Application to skin and mucous membrane.
Protection from infection of healthcare staff only.
Protection from infection of patients only.
questions.explanation: Standard precautions apply to blood, all body fluids, secretions, excretions, non-intact skin, and mucous membranes to protect both patients and staff.

questions.stem: The 'first moment' in the Five Moments for Hand Hygiene occurs when:
options: After patient contact/on leaving the point of care.
Before you put on personal protective equipment (i.e. gloves/aprons).
Before patient contact as possible within the patient zone.
Before you start to gather the equipment that you need to take to the patient's bedside.
questions.explanation: The WHO 'My 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene' begins with Moment 1: Before touching a patient (upon entering the patient zone).

questions.stem: Rate of transmission of HCV after needle stick injury is:
questions.explanation: Remember the 'Rule of 3s' for needlestick injuries: HBV ~30%, HCV ~3% (1.8–3%), and HIV ~0.3%.

questions.stem: A neonate presents with chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcifications. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: The classic triad of congenital toxoplasmosis is chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications.

questions.stem: The drug of choice for treatment of toxoplasmosis is:
questions.explanation: Synergistic therapy with Pyrimethamine plus Sulfadiazine (with Folinic acid/leucovorin to prevent bone marrow suppression) is the gold-standard treatment for toxoplasmosis.

questions.stem: The most common route of human infection with Toxoplasma gondii is:
options: Ingestion of undercooked meat containing tissue cysts
questions.explanation: Ingestion of undercooked meat (pork, lamb) containing Toxoplasma tissue cysts (bradyzoites) or oocysts from cat feces are the primary transmission routes.

questions.stem: Which population is particularly at risk of severe complications from toxoplasmosis?
questions.explanation: Toxoplasmosis is usually asymptomatic in immunocompetent hosts but causes severe fetal damage in primary maternal infection and encephalitis in AIDS/immunocompromised patients.

questions.stem: A 44-Year old women with HIV positive CD4 count 73 presents with progressive left side hemiplegia and headache over a week MRI brain showing multiple ring- enhancing mass lesions with surrounding cerebral edema the most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions with surrounding edema in an AIDS patient (CD4 <100) are most commonly caused by reactivation of Cerebral Toxoplasmosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding toxoplasmosis is true:
options: It is a type of flagellate.
Congenital toxoplasmosis results in optic nerve atrophy.
The cat is the only known animal reservoir.
questions.explanation: In immunocompetent individuals, primary Toxoplasma gondii infection is typically asymptomatic or a mild, self-limiting mononucleosis-like illness.

questions.stem: Toxoplasmosis is infection with Toxoplasma gondii. The only known hosts of this organism are domestic cats and their relatives. Which of the following is the most common mode of infection in humans?
questions.explanation: Following the prompt's emphasis on domestic cats as definitive hosts, humans acquire infection via ingestion of sporulated oocysts shed in cat feces.

questions.stem: Infection with T. gondii can manifest in many different ways. Which of the following types of toxoplasmosis results from congenital infection that is reactivated in a patient's late teens or 20s?
questions.explanation: Congenital toxoplasmosis frequently remains subclinical at birth and reactivates in the 2nd or 3rd decade of life as recurrent ocular chorioretinitis.

questions.stem: What things can you get from a restaurant that will cause you to gain this parasite (Toxoplasma gondii)?
questions.explanation: Both undercooked meat (harboring tissue cysts) and unwashed raw vegetables/salads (contaminated with soil oocysts) transmit Toxoplasma gondii.

questions.stem: Toxoplasmosis is diagnosed using an indirect fluorescent antibody (IFA) test or enzyme immunoassay (EIA) for IgG or IgM antibodies. Which of the following results of serologic testing for T. gondii indicates that a patient has a possible acute infection?
options: IgG is equivocal; IgM is positive
IgG is positive; IgM is equivocal
IgG is positive; IgM is negative
questions.explanation: Positive anti-Toxoplasma IgM with negative/equivocal IgG indicates early acute primary infection (IgG rises 1–2 weeks later).

questions.stem: If prenatal diagnosis reveals infection in the fetus, the pregnant patient should receive
questions.explanation: Spiramycin prevents placental transmission before fetal infection; once fetal infection is confirmed (after 18 weeks), Pyrimethamine + Sulfadiazine + Folinic acid is required.

questions.stem: The most common mode of transmission of health care associated infection is:
questions.explanation: Direct and indirect contact transmission—predominantly via the unwashed hands of healthcare personnel—is the leading route of nosocomial infections.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an adverse effect of fluoroquinolones?
questions.explanation: Fluoroquinolones cause QTc prolongation, dysglycemia, tendinitis/Achilles tendon rupture, and CNS effects, whereas aplastic anemia is classically linked to chloramphenicol.

questions.stem: Which of the following risk factors for community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus?
questions.explanation: Injection drug use, crowded facilities, contact sports, and skin trauma are key risk factors for Community-Acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA).

questions.stem: Which adverse reactions would you need to counsel if you prescribe doxycycline?
options: Clostridium difficile infection, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, anaphylaxis
Worsening infection, bone marrow suppression, GI upset
Bone marrow suppression, acute kidney injury
questions.explanation: Patients taking doxycycline must be counseled to use sun protection (photosensitivity) and swallow pills upright with plenty of water (to prevent pill esophagitis).

questions.stem: In addition to the evaluation of signs and symptoms on presentation, which of the following tests would be most helpful to diagnose a patient with a diabetic foot infection?
questions.explanation: MRI is the most sensitive and specific imaging modality to detect deep soft-tissue abscesses and underlying osteomyelitis in diabetic foot infections.

questions.stem: What pathogen(s) is/are the most common cause of vertebral osteomyelitis?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus accounts for more than 50% of cases of hematogenous pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis.

questions.stem: Antimicrobial prescription guidelines:
options: Should be based on international antimicrobial recommendations
Are unhelpful when implementing antimicrobial stewardship
Give recommendations on antimicrobial selection, dose and duration based on local data
Give recommendations on which brands of antimicrobials to use.
questions.explanation: Effective antimicrobial stewardship guidelines tailor empiric drug selection, dosing, and duration to local institutional antibiograms and resistance patterns.

questions.stem: What test is needed to determine the cause of a central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI)?
questions.explanation: Paired peripheral and central-line blood cultures (assessing differential time to positivity) are essential to diagnose and identify the causative organism of CLABSI.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old man is evaluated in the hospital for fever. He underwent elective coronary artery bypass graft surgery 2 days ago. urinary catheter was inserted in the operating room. Medical history is unremarkable, and he takes no medications. On physical examination, temperature is 38.4 °C, blood pressure is 130/84 mm Hg, pulse rate is 88/min, and respiration rate is 18/min. Lungs are clear to auscultation. The sternotomy incision site is clean and dry. He has mild suprapubic tenderness but no costovertebral angle or flank tenderness. Urine analysis reveals 10 to 20 leukocytes/hpf.Urine culture reveals > 400 colonies gram-negative rods. Chest radiograph shows no infiltrate. In addition to removing the urinary catheter, which of the following is the mostappropriate management?
options: wait antimicrobial sensitivity before beginning antimicrobial therapy
Repeat urinalysis and urine culture in 24 hours
questions.explanation: In a symptomatic febrile post-op patient with suprapubic tenderness, pyuria, and Gram-negative bacteriuria (CAUTI), catheter removal plus immediate empiric antibiotics is indicated.

questions.stem: One of the following bundle has been shown to reduce ventilator associated pneumonia (VAP ) rates:
options: elevate the head of the bed to between 90 and 120 degrees.
no prophylaxis for peptic ulcer is needed.
early ambulation to prevent anti-deep venous thrombosis.
questions.explanation: VAP prevention bundles include head-of-bed elevation (30–45°), daily sedation vacations/weaning readiness, peptic ulcer/DVT prophylaxis, and daily oral care with chlorhexidine.

questions.stem: Rifampicin is used in all except
questions.explanation: Rifampicin is utilized in tuberculosis, leprosy, meningococcal prophylaxis, and severe Legionnaires' disease, whereas bartonellosis is treated with doxycycline/azithromycin/chloramphenicol.

questions.stem: The first line antibiotic for community acquired pneumonia in healthy adults is usually:
questions.explanation: Outpatient community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in previously healthy adults without comorbidities is treated with high-dose Amoxicillin, Doxycycline, or a Macrolide (Azithromycin).

questions.stem: The following organism is a frequent cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia?
questions.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (along with MRSA and Enterobacterales) is a major multidrug-resistant cause of hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions is typically present in patients with chronic bronchitis but absent in patients with acute bronchitis?
options: Past medical history of multiple respiratory infections
Presence of reversible airflow limitation on spirometry testing
questions.explanation: Chronic productive cough with mucopurulent sputum (>=3 months/year for >=2 consecutive years) characterizes chronic bronchitis (COPD), whereas acute bronchitis is typically viral and self-limiting.

questions.stem: What is the appropriate total duration of therapy (days) of antibiotic(s) for community acquired pneumonia?
questions.explanation: IDSA/ATS guidelines recommend a minimum total antibiotic duration of 5 days for uncomplicated CAP provided the patient is afebrile for 48–72h and clinically stable.

questions.stem: A patient is to begin IV antibiotic therapy for a pulmonary infection, what should be completed before the first dose of antibiotic is administered?
questions.explanation: Microbiological specimens (sputum and blood cultures) should be collected prior to administering the first IV antibiotic dose so culture yield is not sterilized.

questions.stem: The primary preventive strategy for community-acquired pneumonia is:
options: Immunization with pneumococcal and influenza vaccines.
questions.explanation: Vaccination with pneumococcal conjugate/polysaccharide vaccines and annual influenza immunization is the cornerstone of CAP primary prevention.

questions.stem: The single most useful clinical sign of severity of pneumonia in a person without underlying lung disease is:
options: Postural fall of SBP >10 mm Hg.
questions.explanation: Tachypnea with a respiratory rate >30 breaths/minute is a core CURB-65 severity criterion and the earliest sensitive clinical indicator of respiratory compromise.

questions.stem: Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) is defined as pneumonia occurring how many hours after hospital admission?
questions.explanation: Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) is defined as pneumonia developing >=48 hours after hospital admission that was not incubating at the time of admission.

questions.stem: Which bacterial pathogen is most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia in adults?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) remains the single most common bacterial etiology of community-acquired pneumonia across all adult age groups.

questions.stem: Drug of choice in pneumonic legionellosis is
questions.explanation: Intracellular Legionella pneumophila requires macrolides (Erythromycin/Azithromycin) or respiratory fluoroquinolones; beta-lactams are completely ineffective.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old ICU patient developed septic shock due to pseudomonas infection Despite IV fluids, his MAP is less than 65 mmHg. Best next step is:
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor of choice in septic shock to restore Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) >= 65 mmHg after fluid resuscitation.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old febrile patient developed sepsis after urinary tract infection, the most common causative organism is:
questions.explanation: Escherichia coli is the leading Gram-negative bacillus responsible for urosepsis and community-acquired Gram-negative bacteremia.

questions.stem: The surviving sepsis campaign recommends which of the following as part of initial management:
options: Broad spectrum antibiotics within one hour
questions.explanation: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle mandates administering broad-spectrum IV antimicrobials within 1 hour of sepsis recognition alongside blood cultures and crystalloid resuscitation.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true regarding Staphylococcus aureus infective endocarditis?
options: S. aureus is the most common causative organism of IE in adults
Mortality rates associated with S. aureus IE range from 20% to 45%
Blood cultures should be repeated to confirm if this is a contaminant or a true pathogen
All of the above are true
questions.explanation: S. aureus is the leading cause of acute infective endocarditis worldwide, carries high mortality (20–45%), and requires serial blood cultures to document persistent bacteremia and clearance.

questions.stem: 70 years old man came to emergency with septic shock, which empiric antimicrobial therapy is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Empiric therapy for undifferentiated septic shock requires broad anti-MRSA coverage (Vancomycin) plus an antipseudomonal beta-lactam (Cefepime or Piperacillin-tazobactam).

questions.stem: Which of the following is true regarding neutropenic fever?
options: An oral temperature of 37.8°C represents a fever
Common signs and symptoms of infection are often absent
Febrile neutropenia is more common in solid tumor patients compared to acute leukemia patients
Chemotherapy-induced mucositis is an uncommon cause of neutropenic fever.
questions.explanation: Because neutrophils are severely depleted, classic inflammatory signs (pus, fluctuation, exudates, infiltrates) are blunted or absent, making fever the sole warning sign.

questions.stem: Which of the following is accurate about the workup of infective endocarditis?
options: The presence of a continuous bacteremia is sufficient to diagnose an infected valvular vegetation
The criterion standard test for diagnosing infective endocarditis is documentation of continuous bacteremia (>30 minutes) on the basis of blood culture results
Leukocytosis is commonly observed in subacute endocarditis, with anemia common in acute endocarditis
questions.explanation: Demonstrating persistent/continuous bacteremia via multiple positive blood culture sets drawn >30 minutes apart is a major Duke criterion and hallmark of intravascular endocardial infection.

questions.stem: A 36years old menstruating female appears in the emergency room with fever (40 C), leukocytosis, BP: 90/65 - rash on her trunk palms & soles. She is diagnosed as a toxic shock syndrome case. Which of the following virulence factors is responsible for these manifestations?
questions.explanation: In this exam key, toxin-mediated systemic cytokine storm (TSST-1 superantigen / pyrogenic exotoxin, keyed as Endotoxin here) drives fever, hypotension, and diffuse erythroderma.

questions.stem: Most reliable clue to poor tissue perfusion in septic shock is:
questions.explanation: Elevated serum lactate (>2 mmol/L) reflects cellular anaerobic glycolysis and is the most reliable biomarker of global tissue hypoperfusion in septic shock.

questions.stem: In neutropenic fever, absolute count of neutrophils is:
questions.explanation: Severe neutropenia in febrile neutropenia is defined as an Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC) <= 500 cells/mm³ (or <1000 expected to fall <=500 within 48h).

questions.stem: The filarial larva can be collected from sample of:
questions.explanation: Wuchereria bancrofti microfilariae exhibit nocturnal periodicity, appearing in maximum concentration in peripheral blood between 10 PM and 2 AM (midnight).

questions.stem: The following does not describe lymphatic filariasis:
options: Caused by Brugia malayi and Wuchereria bancrofti
questions.explanation: Lymphatic filariasis is transmitted by mosquitoes (Culex, Anopheles, Aedes)—NOT molluscs/snails (which are intermediate hosts for trematodes like Schistosoma).

questions.stem: Microfilariae of Wuchereria bancrofti show:
questions.explanation: Wuchereria bancrofti microfilariae reside in pulmonary capillaries during the day and enter peripheral blood at night (nocturnal periodicity) to coincide with Culex mosquito feeding.

questions.stem: Rift valley fever virus primarily affects which organ in severe human disease?
questions.explanation: Severe Rift Valley Fever (Phlebovirus) characteristically causes fulminant hepatic necrosis/hemorrhagic fever and ocular retinitis/macular edema leading to visual loss.

questions.stem: The diagnostic test of choice for detecting microfilariae of W. bancrofti is:
questions.explanation: A Giemsa-stained thick peripheral blood smear collected at night (10 PM–2 AM) is the classic diagnostic test to visualize sheathed W. bancrofti microfilariae.

questions.stem: What drug is used to treat lymphatic filariasis caused by Wuchereria bancrofti except:
questions.explanation: Diethylcarbamazine (DEC), Ivermectin, and Doxycycline (which kills symbiotic Wolbachia bacteria) treat filariasis; Atebrine (quinacrine) is an antimalarial/anti-giardial agent.

questions.stem: Ribavirin may be active against the following viral hemorrhagic fever virus:
questions.explanation: Ribavirin demonstrates antiviral activity against bunyaviruses and arenaviruses, including Rift Valley Fever, Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever, and Lassa fever.

questions.stem: Mosquitoes are the vector in the following disorders
questions.explanation: Bancroftian filariasis is transmitted by mosquitoes (Culex/Anopheles), whereas onchocerciasis (blackfly), leishmaniasis (sandfly), and trypanosomiasis (tsetse fly) have other vectors.

questions.stem: One of the following is not a typical feature of tropical pulmonary eosinophilia:
questions.explanation: Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE) is an occult hypersensitivity response to trapped microfilariae in the lungs; circulating blood microfilariae are characteristically ABSENT.

questions.stem: Which one of the following viral diseases is transmitted by blood-sucking insects and contact with sheep & cattle?
questions.explanation: Rift Valley fever is transmitted to humans via Aedes/Culex mosquito bites or direct contact with blood/tissues of infected sheep, goats, and cattle.

questions.stem: Under the One Health framework, which is a key preventive strategy for zoonoses?
options: Surveillance of animal populations and environmental reservoirs
questions.explanation: One Health integrates human, animal, and environmental health surveillance to detect and control zoonotic spillovers at their animal/ecological source.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct regarding zoonotic viral emerging infections?
options: They are always caused by viruses that are new to humans
They often spill over from animals and may mutate for human-to-human spread
They usually have stable transmission and low mutation rates
They never cause epidemics or pandemic
questions.explanation: Emerging RNA zoonotic viruses frequently spill over from wildlife reservoirs and undergo adaptive mutations enabling efficient human-to-human epidemic spread.

questions.stem: One of the best example of organisms causing One Health Disease is:
questions.explanation: Brucella abortus is a quintessential zoonotic 'One Health' pathogen transmitted between livestock (cattle) and humans via unpasteurized dairy or occupational contact.

questions.stem: What category of bioterrorism agents does the CDC characterize as easily transmitted from animal to person, have a high mortality rate, and include Anthrax, plague, and Ebola?
questions.explanation: CDC Category A bioterrorism agents pose the highest national security risk due to ease of dissemination, high mortality, and public health impact (Anthrax, Plague, Botulism, Smallpox, Tularemia, Viral Hemorrhagic Fevers).

questions.stem: A 46-years old man presents three days after returning from safari holiday in Nigeria complaining of fever, chills, myalgia and malaise who started 2 days ago now complaining of day time somnolence and night time insomnia and acting strangely at home, HIV test is negative. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Inversion of the sleep-wake cycle (daytime somnolence and nighttime insomnia) with neuropsychiatric changes after an African safari is classic for Human African Trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness).

questions.stem: Which of the following are the reservoirs for the flea-born typhus called murine typhus:
questions.explanation: Endemic (murine) typhus is caused by Rickettsia typhi, maintained in rat reservoirs and transmitted to humans by the rat flea (Xenopsylla cheopis).

questions.stem: A 36-Year old female presents to the Emergency department with fever, chest pain and hemoptysis. She comes from visit to her family where she is working in wool processing centre. Chest x-ray show wide mediastinum, sputum and blood cultures revealing gram-positive rods. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Wool-sorting exposure, hemorrhagic mediastinitis causing pathognomonic mediastinal widening on CXR, and large spore-forming Gram-positive bacilli confirm Inhalational Anthrax.

questions.stem: Rat-bite fever is caused by the organism:
questions.explanation: Rat-bite fever is caused by Spirillum minus (sodoku, common in Asia) or Streptobacillus moniliformis (common in North America).

questions.stem: Nipah is a zoonotic paramyxovirus; where did it originate?
questions.explanation: Fruit bats of the genus Pteropus (flying foxes) are the natural wildlife reservoir of Nipah virus, which spilled over into pigs and humans.

questions.stem: Woolsorter's disease is:
questions.explanation: Inhalational anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) is historically termed 'Woolsorter's disease' due to inhalation of spores from contaminated goat hair and sheep wool.

questions.stem: Which of the following antibiotic combination is commonly used in triple therapy of H. pylori infection:
questions.explanation: Standard first-line triple therapy for Helicobacter pylori consists of a Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI) + Clarithromycin + Amoxicillin (or Metronidazole if penicillin-allergic).

questions.stem: Which one of the following is the most sensitive and specific test for H. Pylori infection before starting therapy?
options: Rapid urease test for gastric biopsy
questions.explanation: The 13C/14C Urea Breath Test is the most accurate non-invasive test (>95% sensitivity and specificity) for detecting active H. pylori infection.

questions.stem: Which of the following is preferred as initial diagnostic test for H pylori:
questions.explanation: In young dyspeptic patients without alarm symptoms ('test-and-treat' strategy), the non-invasive Urea Breath Test (or stool antigen) is preferred initially.

questions.stem: People with Helicobacter pylori infection are 3 to 6 times more likely to develop stomach cancer. Which of the following cancers is NOT associated with H. pylori infection?
questions.explanation: H. pylori strongly increases the risk of non-cardia gastric adenocarcinoma (antrum/body) and gastric MALT lymphoma, but is NOT associated with (and may inversely correlate with) gastric cardia cancer.

questions.stem: Which is accurate about testing for H pylori infection?
options: The H pylori fecal antigen test is highly specific but lacks sensitivity
H pylori serology is useful for follow-up of treated patients
Testing is indicated in all patients with gastro esophageal reflux disease
Unexplained iron deficiency anemia is an indication for H pylori testing
questions.explanation: Unexplained iron-deficiency anemia (along with peptic ulcer disease, MALT lymphoma, and uninvestigated dyspepsia) is a well-established clinical indication for H. pylori testing.

questions.stem: A young woman undergoes upper endoscopy for unexplained nausea, and vomiting,the stomach appears normal. Surveillance gastric biopsies are taken and the gastric biopsies ureate test is positive. The biopsies are most likely to show:
options: Helicobacter pylori organism, but no gastric or esophageal inflammation
Helicobacter pylori organism plus gastric inflammation (gastritis)
Neither Helicobacter pylori organisms, nor inflammation because the ureate test is often false positive with a normal endoscopy
questions.explanation: Virtually all individuals colonized with Helicobacter pylori exhibit histologic chronic active gastritis on biopsy even when macroscopic endoscopic mucosa appears normal.

questions.stem: What is the most likely commonest source for humans to acquire H. pylori infection?
options: Contact with infected secretion from other people
questions.explanation: H. pylori is primarily transmitted person-to-person via gastro-oral, oral-oral (saliva/vomitus), or fecal-oral contact with infected human secretions.

questions.stem: In the developed world, seroprevalence of Helicobacter pylori infection is currently:
questions.explanation: Improved sanitation, clean water, and widespread eradication therapy have steadily decreased H. pylori seroprevalence in developed nations.

questions.stem: A 24 years old male coming to you complaining of epigastic discomfort and vomiting,You requested testing for H.pylori which was positive .In addition to PPI .Choose the most suitable antimicrobials
questions.explanation: Clarithromycin and Amoxicillin combined with a PPI constitute the standard triple eradication regimen for confirmed H. pylori gastritis.

questions.stem: Referring to the last question (24-year-old male treated for H. pylori with PPI + Clarithromycin & Amoxicillin), one month after receiving a 14-day course of the antimicrobials, you prescribed for Helicobacter pylori. He still has mild dyspepsia and pain after meals. What is the appropriate next step in management?
options: Empirical long-term proton pump inhibitor therapy
Endoscopy with biopsy to rule out gastric adenocarcinoma
Second-line therapy for H. pylori with omeprazole, bismuth subsalicylate, tetracycline, and metronidazole
questions.explanation: At >=4 weeks post-therapy (after stopping PPIs for 2 weeks), a non-invasive Urea Breath Test (or stool antigen test) is performed to confirm eradication before initiating second-line quadruple therapy.

questions.stem: The recommended antibiotic combination to treat brucellosis is:
questions.explanation: WHO-recommended first-line combination therapy for human brucellosis is Doxycycline plus Rifampicin (for 6 weeks) to prevent relapse of intracellular organisms.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most characteristic of brucellosis?
questions.explanation: Brucellosis ('undulant fever') classically presents with subacute/chronic undulating fevers, drenching night sweats (often with a musty odor), arthralgias, and back pain.

questions.stem: 39-years old man farmer complaining for an 8- weeks off intermittent fever which rise in the afternoon and fall during night, fatigue, muscle, joint and low back pain, examination shows hepatomegaly and low back pain is elicited with flexion and distention What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Farming occupation, 8-week undulating fever, sacroiliitis/low back pain, and hepatomegaly are textbook features of Brucellosis.

questions.stem: What is the main virulence factor of Brucella?
questions.explanation: Brucella is a Gram-negative coccobacillus lacking exotoxins and capsules; its smooth lipopolysaccharide (LPS) endotoxin contributes to virulence and intracellular survival in macrophages.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old veterinarian presents with malaise, chills, sweats, fatigue and intermittent fever. Most likely etiologic agent?
questions.explanation: Veterinarians, abattoir workers, and farmers exposed to livestock birth tissues or unpasteurized milk are at high occupational risk for Brucella abortus/melitensis.

questions.stem: The most reliable test in diagnosis of Brucellosis is:
options: Isolation of organism from lymph nodes
questions.explanation: While blood/bone marrow culture is definitive, the Standard Serum Agglutination Test (SAT, titre >=1:160) is the most widely used and reliable rapid diagnostic test in clinical practice.

questions.stem: Patient with intermittent fever presents with features treated successfully with doxycycline and rifampicin, probable diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Intermittent undulant fever responding to a 6-week course of Doxycycline + Rifampicin confirms Brucellosis.

questions.stem: Malta fever is caused by:
questions.explanation: Brucellosis is historically known as Malta fever, Mediterranean fever, or Undulant fever, caused by Brucella species (B. melitensis, B. abortus).

questions.stem: Which is false regarding brucellosis
options: Acquired through contact or ingestion of raw goat's milk
Brucella melitensis is the most common type of infection
CFT is more important in acute infection than agglutination reaction
May present as pyrexia of unknown origin
questions.explanation: Standard Agglutination Test (SAT / IgM) is diagnostic in acute brucellosis, whereas Complement Fixation Test (CFT / IgG) becomes more useful in chronic brucellosis.

questions.stem: Male patient 29 years old, butcher, presented to OPC by fever, days of fever followed by days without fever, associated with profuse sweating and back pain. His CBC showed mild anemia and leukocytosis. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Occupational meat/animal contact (butcher), undulating fever, profuse sweating, and osteoarticular back pain (sacroiliitis) point directly to Brucellosis.

questions.stem: Chemoprophylaxis is :-
options: Antigenic preparations in the form of organisms or toxoid
Already formed antibodies to induce humoral or cellular immunity
Antimicrobial drugs given just before or immediately after exposure
System of preserving vaccines, toxoid, and sera
questions.explanation: Chemoprophylaxis is the administration of antimicrobial agents before or immediately following exposure to prevent infection or clinical disease (e.g., Rifampicin for meningococcal contacts).

questions.stem: An example of secondary prevention is:
options: Detection of asymptomatic cases of diabetes mellitus
questions.explanation: Secondary prevention focuses on early detection and prompt treatment of subclinical/asymptomatic disease via screening (e.g., screening for asymptomatic diabetes or hypertension).

questions.stem: Giving routine iron and folic acid to all pregnant women is a form of:
questions.explanation: Nutritional supplementation (iron and folic acid) in healthy pregnant women prevents maternal anemia and neural tube defects before disease occurs—constituting Primary Prevention.

questions.stem: Seroprophylaxis is: -
options: Antigenic preparations in the form of organisms or toxoide.
Already formed antibodies to induce Humoral or Cellular immunity.
Antimicrobial drugs given just before or immediately after exposure.
System of preserving vaccines, toxoid, and sera.
questions.explanation: Seroprophylaxis provides immediate passive immunity using preformed antibodies (immune globulins or antisera such as HBIG, RIG, or TIG).

questions.stem: Community control includes the following except:-
questions.explanation: In community medicine classification, concurrent/terminal disinfection is a patient/case-level control measure, whereas sanitation, health education, and mass immunization are community-wide measures.

questions.stem: Adequate treatment of a case is considered as:
options: Primary prevention for case and contact
Primary prevention for case and secondary for contact
Secondary prevention for case and primary for contact
questions.explanation: Early diagnosis and prompt adequate treatment of an infected patient halts disease progression and complications—defining Secondary Prevention of the case.

questions.stem: Primary prevention refers to:
options: Measures carried out for healthy individuals.
Measures taken after occurrence of the disease.
Measures taken after occurrence of complications.
questions.explanation: Primary prevention encompasses health promotion and specific protection (e.g., immunization, sanitation) applied to healthy susceptible individuals prior to disease onset.

questions.stem: The level of prevention that takes place during the early phases of pathogenesis and includes activities that limit the progression of disease is:
questions.explanation: Secondary prevention intervenes during the early pathogenic stage through screening and prompt treatment to arrest disease progression.

questions.stem: The following are primary preventive measures EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Early diagnosis and prompt treatment constitute Secondary Prevention, whereas vaccination, health education, and nutrition are Primary Prevention.

questions.stem: According to WHO classification, a category III of rabies exposure requires:
questions.explanation: WHO Category III rabies exposure (transdermal bites/scratches, licks on broken skin, bat exposure) in unvaccinated individuals requires wound washing + Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG) + full rabies vaccine series.

questions.stem: According to WHO classification, a category III of rabies exposure (eg: tissue dermal bite or licking of broken skin) in patients who have been previously immunized, which of the following is required:
questions.explanation: Previously immunized individuals already have immunological memory; they require wound cleansing and 2 booster doses of rabies vaccine (days 0 and 3) WITHOUT Rabies Immunoglobulin.

questions.stem: A young boy was playing with a kitten and now has cat scratch disease. Which bacteria species is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Bartonella henselae (a pleomorphic Gram-negative bacillus transmitted by kitten scratches/bites or cat fleas) is the causative agent of Cat Scratch Disease.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old man is bitten by a forest dog. What is the most appropriate advice after thorough cleansing of the wound?
options: Give human rabies immunoglobulin + full course of vaccination
Give human rabies immunoglobulin + oral penicillin for the next 2 weeks
Advise low risk but take oral co-amoxiclav for the dog bite
questions.explanation: Bites from wild or stray/forest dogs represent high-risk Category III exposure requiring immediate wound washing, Human Rabies Immunoglobulin (HRIG), and full rabies vaccination.

questions.stem: As regard rabies vaccine for non-immunized adults:
options: Vaccine HDCV or PCECV 1.0 mL, IM (deltoid area), one each on days 0 and 3
Vaccine HDCV or PCECV 1.0 mL, IM (deltoid area), one each on days 0, 3, 7, and 14.
Anterolateral aspect of the thigh is preferred
questions.explanation: Post-exposure rabies vaccination in non-immunized immunocompetent adults consists of 4 IM doses (1.0 mL HDCV or PCECV) into the deltoid muscle on days 0, 3, 7, and 14 (plus RIG on day 0).

questions.stem: An 18-year-old man is bitten by a frantic dog whilst taking a gap year in Ecuador. He is worried about rabies and phones for advice. He was not immunised against rabies prior to travelling to Ecuador. What is the most appropriate advice after thorough cleansing of the wound?
options: Give human rabies immunoglobulin + full course vaccination.
Give human rabies immunoglobulin + oral penicillin for 2 weeks.
questions.explanation: An unprovoked bite by a frantic/rabid-appearing dog in an unvaccinated traveler requires both passive immunity (HRIG infiltrated around the wound) and active vaccination.

questions.stem: Cat-scratch disease is characterized by all except:
questions.explanation: Cat-scratch disease causes subacute regional lymphadenopathy, positive Hanger-Rose skin test, and occasional erythema nodosum; it is usually self-limiting (or treated with azithromycin), NOT systemic corticosteroids.

questions.stem: Which type of bite represents a potential medical emergency in an asplenic patient?
questions.explanation: Dog saliva harbors Capnocytophaga canimorsus, which can cause fulminant, rapidly fatal septic shock and purpura fulminans in asplenic or cirrhotic patients.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old previously healthy female letter carrier works in an area in which the presence of rabid foxes have been documented. She is bitten by a bat, which then flies away. Initial examination reveals a clean break in the skin in the right upper forearm. She has no history of receiving treatment for rabies and is unsure about vaccination against tetanus. The physician should:
options: cleans the wound with a 20% soap solution
cleans the wound with a 20% soap solution and administer tetanus toxoid
cleans the wound with a 20% soap solution, administer tetanus toxoid, and administer human rabies immune globulin intramuscularly
clean the wound with a 20% soap solution, administer tetanus toxoid, administer human rabies immune globulin IM, and administer human diploid cell vaccine
clean the wound with a 20% soap solution and administer human diploid cell vaccine
questions.explanation: Bat bites are high-risk rabies exposures; comprehensive management includes thorough soap-and-water cleansing, tetanus toxoid booster, HRIG, and HDCV rabies vaccine.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most characteristic of classical dengue fever?
options: Acute high-grade fever, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, and rash
questions.explanation: Classical dengue ('breakbone fever') presents abruptly with high fever, severe retro-orbital headache, intense myalgias/arthralgias, leukopenia/thrombocytopenia, and a maculopapular rash.

questions.stem: All of the following causing hemorrhagic fever EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) and aplastic crisis—not viral hemorrhagic fever, unlike Rift Valley, Yellow Fever, and Dengue viruses.

questions.stem: All the following are criteria of Viral hemorrhagic fever except:
questions.explanation: Most viral hemorrhagic fevers (e.g., Dengue, Yellow fever, Ebola, Marburg) have NO specific curative antiviral treatment and rely primarily on intensive supportive care.

questions.stem: The most prevalent worldwide mosquito borne viral infection is:
questions.explanation: Dengue virus (transmitted by Aedes aegypti) is the most widespread arboviral infection globally, affecting ~100–400 million people annually across the tropics.

questions.stem: 30-year-old man returned from Saudi Arabia with fever, joint pain, myalgia and retro-orbital headache. Most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Dengue fever is endemic in western Saudi Arabia (Jeddah/Makkah) and presents with acute fever, severe arthralgia/myalgia, and retro-orbital pain.

questions.stem: As regard dengue fever which is not true:
options: Is spread by the vector aedes aegypti
Has an incubation period of 2-3 weeks
Is the cause of hemorrhagic fever
questions.explanation: Dengue fever has a short intrinsic incubation period of 4 to 7 days (range 3–10 days), NOT 2–3 weeks.

questions.stem: How does Ebola spread from human to human?
options: Spreads through direct contact with blood and bodily fluids.
questions.explanation: Ebola virus spreads human-to-human via direct contact (through broken skin or mucous membranes) with blood, secretions, organs, or bodily fluids of infected persons.

questions.stem: A 30 years man from Australia returned from a business trip to Indonesia 6d ago presenting with complaints of fever, joint and muscle ache and headache, in particular behind the eye for the past 2 days. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Travel to Southeast Asia (Indonesia) 4–6 days prior with acute fever, severe myalgias/arthralgias, and retro-orbital pain is textbook Dengue fever.

questions.stem: Because prompt identification of the cause of encephalitis via PCR is difficult treatment should not be withheld pending test results and should consist of:
questions.explanation: Empiric intravenous Acyclovir must be initiated immediately in any patient with suspected viral encephalitis to treat potentially fatal Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) encephalitis.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with high-grade fever, confusion and seizures. MRI shows temporal lobe involvement. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Herpes Simplex Virus type 1 (HSV-1) characteristically produces hemorrhagic necrosis and edema of the inferior and medial temporal lobes on brain MRI.

questions.stem: Which of the following acyclovir regimens should be started for viral encephalitis?
options: Acyclovir 400 mg PO five times daily
Acyclovir 800 mg PO five times daily
questions.explanation: Viral/HSV encephalitis requires high-dose parenteral therapy: IV Acyclovir 10 mg/kg (approx. 600–750 mg) every 8 hours for 14–21 days.

questions.stem: Encephalitis manifested by the followings except:
questions.explanation: Encephalitis manifests with altered sensorium, focal deficits, seizures, and systemic/arboviral signs (rash, hemorrhagic epistaxis), whereas dysuria and pyuria indicate a UTI.

questions.stem: A 50-Years old develop sudden onset of bizarre behavior, CSF shows lymphocytes MRI show temporal lobe abnormality, what is the etiology:
questions.explanation: Acute personality/behavioral changes, temporal lobe MRI lesions, and lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis are pathognomonic for Herpes Simplex Virus encephalitis.

questions.stem: Inflammation of the brain parenchyma is referred to as:
questions.explanation: Encephalitis denotes direct inflammation of the brain parenchyma (manifesting with altered consciousness, personality changes, and focal neurological deficits).

questions.stem: Regarding primary amoebic meningoencephalitis, which is false?
options: Acquired by swimming in fresh warm water
questions.explanation: Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (Naegleria fowleri) is treated with Amphotericin B + Miltefosine + Azoles/Rifampin; dehydroemetine is ineffective because it does not cross the blood-brain barrier.

questions.stem: An enzyme that is important for viral release from host cell through the viral life cycle:
questions.explanation: Influenza neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid residues on host cell surfaces, allowing newly formed virions to bud and release; oseltamivir and zanamivir inhibit this enzyme.

questions.stem: Entecavir has antiviral action in treatment of HBV through inhibition of the enzyme:
questions.explanation: Entecavir is a guanosine nucleoside analog that competitively inhibits HBV reverse transcriptase (DNA polymerase), blocking viral replication.

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate duration of therapy for uncomplicated influenza treated with oseltamivir?
questions.explanation: Standard treatment for acute uncomplicated influenza with oral Oseltamivir (75 mg twice daily) is 5 days, started within 48 hours of symptom onset.

questions.stem: Which antiviral drug is commonly used to treat severe CMV infections?
questions.explanation: Intravenous Ganciclovir (or oral Valganciclovir) is the first-line antiviral agent for severe Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis, colitis, and pneumonitis.

questions.stem: Zidovudine is used in the treatment of HIV and acts through inhibition of:
questions.explanation: Zidovudine (AZT) is a thymidine nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) that causes chain termination of proviral HIV DNA.

questions.stem: daclatasvir is useful in the treatment of HCV and acts through:
questions.explanation: Daclatasvir inhibits the HCV NS5A non-structural protein, blocking both viral RNA replication complex formation and virion assembly.

questions.stem: Acyclovir is an antiviral drug that is usually used in treatment of:
questions.explanation: Acyclovir is selectively phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase in Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) and Varicella-Zoster Virus (Herpes Zoster) infected cells.

questions.stem: Which zoonotic disease is associated with camels?
questions.explanation: Dromedary camels are the primary zoonotic intermediate reservoir transmitting Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus (MERS-CoV) to humans.

questions.stem: All of the following are skin manifestations of COVID-19 except:
questions.explanation: Recognized cutaneous manifestations of SARS-CoV-2 include pseudo-chilblains ('COVID toes'), urticarial, vesicular, and maculopapular rashes—not lichen planus.

questions.stem: Severe acute respiratory syndrome is caused by?
questions.explanation: Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) is caused by SARS-CoV, an enveloped positive-sense single-stranded RNA Coronavirus.

questions.stem: A patient is being admitted to a medical unit diagnosed COVID 19 which type of room should be assigned by the nurse:
options: Room with window that can be opened
questions.explanation: Patients with COVID-19 (especially when undergoing aerosol-generating procedures) should be placed in an Airborne Infection Isolation Room (AIIR) with negative air pressure.

questions.stem: One of the modern-day worries is about emerging infections. Which of the following is an emerging infection with the greatest global impact?
questions.explanation: Coronaviruses (SARS / SARS-CoV-2) represent the modern emerging respiratory viral pathogens with unprecedented global pandemic impact.

questions.stem: SARS is described as a zoonotic virus. What does this mean?
options: They emerge from animals to cross the species barrier infrequently
Such viruses are confined to animals
They do not cause disease in humans
questions.explanation: Zoonotic viruses originate in animal reservoirs (such as horseshoe bats and palm civets for SARS-CoV) and periodically cross the species barrier to infect humans.

questions.stem: The best diagnostic sample for visceral leishmaniasis is obtained from:
questions.explanation: Splenic aspirate (>95% sensitivity) or bone marrow aspirate (~70–85% sensitivity) demonstrating intracellular Leishmania amastigotes (LD bodies) is the diagnostic gold standard for visceral leishmaniasis.

questions.stem: The treatment of choice for visceral leishmaniasis in most endemic areas is:
options: All of the above, depending on region and resistance
questions.explanation: Liposomal Amphotericin B, Pentavalent antimonials (sodium stibogluconate), and oral Miltefosine are all primary regimens selected based on geographic resistance patterns.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the primary mode of transmission of Leishmaniasis to human?
questions.explanation: Leishmania promastigotes are transmitted to humans through the bite of infected female phlebotomine sandflies (Phlebotomus in Old World, Lutzomyia in New World).

questions.stem: A-21-Years old student coming from trip to Brazil with non-healing ulcer on his face the diagnosis of Leishmania braziliensis is confirmed by biopsy what is the most appropriate treatment:
questions.explanation: New World mucocutaneous species (Leishmania braziliensis) carry risk of destructive nasopharyngeal espundia and require systemic therapy (Liposomal Amphotericin B or systemic antimonials) rather than local cryotherapy.

questions.stem: Which one of the following features is least likely to occur in a patient with visceral leishmaniasis?
questions.explanation: Visceral leishmaniasis ('kala-azar' = black fever) classically causes massive hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, prolonged fever, and hyperpigmented/greyish skin; diarrhea is not a typical hallmark.

questions.stem: Heat acclimatization:
options: Increases the risk of heat injuries
Needs more research before it should even be considered
questions.explanation: Physiological heat acclimatization expands plasma volume, initiates earlier/more dilute sweating, and lowers core temperature and exercise heart rate at a given workload.

questions.stem: Symptoms of heat exhaustion are:
questions.explanation: Heat exhaustion presents with intact thermoregulation, profuse sweating, cool/clammy skin, weakness, and normal/mildly elevated temp (<40°C), whereas heat stroke causes hot dry skin and CNS dysfunction/seizures.

questions.stem: Causes of hypothermia include the following:
questions.explanation: Endocrine causes of impaired thermogenesis and hypothermia include hypothyroidism (myxedema), hypopituitarism, hypoglycemia, and adrenal insufficiency.

questions.stem: Which of the following does not produce hypothermia?
questions.explanation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) produces severe HYPERTHERMIA (along with 'lead-pipe' rigidity and autonomic instability), whereas panhypopituitarism, shock, and myxedema cause hypothermia.

questions.stem: Which of the following produce hypothermia
questions.explanation: Peripheral circulatory failure (shock) impairs tissue perfusion and metabolic heat production, leading to hypothermia, whereas NMS, heat stroke, and thyroid storm cause hyperthermia.

questions.stem: The following viral hemorrhagic fever has WHO approved vaccine for travelers:
questions.explanation: The live-attenuated 17D Yellow Fever vaccine is highly effective, WHO-approved for travelers to endemic regions, and documented on the International Certificate of Vaccination.

questions.stem: Concerning plague:
options: It is caused by Bacillus pestis
The main vector is the rat
The pneumonic form is more common than the bubonic form
Direct person to person spread may occur
questions.explanation: Primary or secondary pneumonic plague (caused by Yersinia pestis, transmitted by rat fleas) can spread directly from person to person via respiratory droplets.

questions.stem: as regard plague which is true:
options: It is caused by bacillus pestis
Pneumonic form is the most common
Person to person transmission may occur
questions.explanation: Yersinia pestis is transmitted by the oriental rat flea (Xenopsylla cheopis), most commonly causes bubonic plague, and exhibits direct person-to-person droplet spread in pneumonic plague.

questions.stem: As regard Yellow fever which is true:
options: has a case fatality rate of 50%
is caused by a flavi virus
epidemics should be controlled by strict isolation of cases
questions.explanation: Yellow fever is caused by an enveloped RNA Flavivirus transmitted by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes (with Councilman bodies seen in the liver).

questions.stem: Faget's sign (relative bradycardia) is first described in
questions.explanation: Faget's sign (pulse-temperature dissociation—falling pulse rate despite rising high fever) was originally described by Dr. Jean Charles Faget in Yellow Fever.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the preferred initial imaging test in suspected liver hydatid cyst?
questions.explanation: Abdominal ultrasonography is the first-line imaging modality of choice for hepatic Echinococcus granulosus hydatid cysts (allowing WHO Gharbi/ultrasound staging and detecting daughter cysts/'hydatid sand').

questions.stem: What is the characteristic pattern seen on X-ray in a patient with suspected Löffler's syndrome?
questions.explanation: Löffler's syndrome (transient larval pulmonary migration of Ascaris, Strongyloides, or hookworms) shows transient, migratory diffuse interstitial/reticulonodular infiltrates with peripheral eosinophilia.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a common parasitic cause of lung infection acquired by eating raw or undercooked crustaceans?
questions.explanation: Paragonimus westermani (oriental lung fluke) is acquired by ingesting raw or undercooked freshwater crabs or crayfish containing metacercariae, causing chronic cough and rusty-brown hemoptysis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false in hydatid disease of liver
options: Caused by larval stage of Echinococcus granulosus
Casoni's test is positive in all
questions.explanation: Casoni's intradermal skin test has low sensitivity and specificity (not positive in all cases) and has been replaced by ultrasound and ELISA serology.
